elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Inserted clause: "Corio may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One". Corio is the Customer-side party (licensee of Commerce One's Software). No Order Form structure exists in this agreement, so Agreement-level coverage is sufficient and the omission of "or any Order Form" / "in whole or in part" is correct surplus avoidance.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One" — exactly 30 days, written, and no additional conditions or approval triggers attached to the election.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "in which case Commerce One shall refund to Corio, pro rata, any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination" — express "pro rata" language, not merely a post-termination-period refund, and the refund direction runs Vendor-to-Customer.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term." Retained §11.2 exits are breach/insolvency only, and the §11.1 notice right operates as natural-term non-renewal effective at expiration (a RENEWAL matter), so no retained mid-term Vendor convenience exit survives.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The inserted right runs on 30 days' notice, not 60-90 days. The fallback is only offered in the margin comment, which is not operative language.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: No early-termination fee cap appears in the operative text; the drafter (correctly for the preferred level) imposed no fee at all, but that leaves the fallback checklist item unaddressed in operative language.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: The insertion prohibits Vendor convenience termination outright rather than permitting it at term end; the fallback formulation is not rendered.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: No 90-day Vendor notice appears; §11.1's non-renewal notice is 30 days before expiration and no Vendor convenience right is granted.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: all four preferred elements are met by the single inserted "Termination for Convenience" paragraph (30 days' written notice, express pro-rata refund of prepaid fees, and an express bar on Vendor convenience termination during the committed term).

The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present: false" reflects the baseline document (original §§11.1-11.2 contain only breach/insolvency and natural-term non-renewal exits) and supports the deviation classification; on inspection of the rendered text the Customer convenience right is in fact present, so the false flag is not a defect in the redline.

Minimality holds: nothing is deleted, no favourable retained language is disturbed, and the insertion adds no survival tail, expense allocation, procedure, or extra damages category. Dropping the model language's "or any Order Form, in whole or in part" is correct because this agreement has no Order Form or partial-termination structure.

Intent preserved: §11.1 term/auto-renewal and §11.2 breach and insolvency exits survive intact. The Vendor bar is drafted as no right to terminate "during" the term, which sits alongside (rather than contradicting) the §11.1 mutual non-renewal notice, whose effect is at expiration of the then-current term.

Drafting hygiene only (not a scoring defect): the new paragraph is unnumbered — number it as §11.3 so the Section 11 cross-referencing scheme stays consistent, and consider adding "Notwithstanding Section 11.1" only if the counterparty argues the renewal-term bar conflicts with its 30-day non-renewal notice; do not add it pre-emptively, as it would be surplus.

Fallback level is not independently satisfied (30-day notice, no fee cap, no Vendor term-end right, no 90-day Vendor notice). That is acceptable because the redline targets the preferred level and only one complete level is required; the fallback is properly offered in the comment rather than in the operative text.
